1. Product Background

1.1 Project Context and Motivation

The IT recruitment market is rapidly shifting toward AI-driven candidate evaluation. Research by Horodyski et al. (2026) highlights that AI is being integrated directly into hiring pipelines through Asynchronous Video Interviews (AVIs) — a format where candidates record their responses independently and submit them for automated algorithmic analysis which may automate or support parts of the initial screening process. This shift creates a new reality: candidates must not only answer correctly in terms of content, but also perform effectively under real-time pressure in front of automated scoring systems. At the core of competency assessment lies Natural Language Processing — the ability to evaluate what a candidate says, how they structure their reasoning, and how they articulate technical knowledge. Since text and audio processing represent this cognitive core, the MVP is deliberately scoped to voice-based interview practice and textual/audio response evaluation. Video-based behavioral analysis (body language, facial expression) is excluded from the MVP as it addresses a secondary signal layer that requires significantly greater infrastructure investment.

For IT students, recent graduates, and early-career IT candidates in Vietnam, this pressure is particularly significant as most have never practiced in a simulated environment resembling these conditions. The gap between technical knowledge taught in university and the ability to communicate it effectively in a real interview remains a largely unaddressed problem. This gap becomes especially critical in the period leading up to enterprise internship cycles (such as OJT phases), when students face rigorous screening rounds for the first time yet have no structured tool to prepare for them.

While general-purpose Large Language Models provide strong natural-language reasoning capabilities, interview evaluation is a domain-constrained task that requires more than fluent text generation. The system must consistently interpret predefined evaluation rubrics, distinguish different levels of answer correctness and completeness, make controlled interview decisions, and generate outputs that follow the same business rules across different interview sessions. Relying entirely on a general-purpose external AI model may introduce variations in scoring, decision making, and response structure because the model has not been specifically optimized for the interview evaluation policies defined by AI-SPEIS.

Therefore, in addition to developing the interview practice platform, AI-SPEIS includes a research-oriented AI component that investigates whether domain-specific fine-tuning can improve the reliability and consistency of interview-related reasoning. A fine-tuned model will be trained on structured datasets representing answer evaluation, interview decisions, question-selection behavior, final feedback, and edge-case handling. The model will operate together with controlled knowledge sources such as the interview question bank and retrieval mechanisms rather than replacing them. Its performance will be evaluated against a general-purpose external AI model under the same predefined test scenarios. This comparison aims to determine whether fine-tuning provides measurable benefits in domain alignment, rule adherence, evaluation consistency, and output reliability for AI-assisted interview practice.

1.2 Real-World Problems Identified from User and HR Stakeholder Research

1.2.1 Target User Survey

To validate the real-world problems addressed by AI-SPEIS, a target user survey was conducted with 236 respondents, including university students, recent graduates, and working candidates. As shown in Figure 1, 62.3% of respondents are current university students, while 37.7% are recent graduates or working candidates. Although university students remain the largest respondent group because they represent the initial target segment of AI-SPEIS, the expanded sample also includes a substantial proportion of respondents with experience or exposure to real-world recruitment. This broader respondent composition helps reduce the risk of interpreting interview preparation needs as being limited only to current university students.

The survey also shows that 72.9% of respondents have participated in at least one internship or job interview, while 81.0% plan to apply for an internship or job within the next six months. Therefore, most respondents either have direct interview experience or have a near-term need to prepare for internship or employment opportunities.

Figure 1 Distribution of survey respondents by current status

The survey highlights several key problems:

Lack of feedback after practice:
Figure 2 shows that 62.7% of respondents reported lacking someone to provide feedback after answering interview questions, while 58.9% reported difficulty determining whether their answers were appropriate. This indicates a clear gap in the post-practice evaluation process, as many respondents do not have a reliable source of feedback to help them identify weaknesses and improve their interview performance.

Difficulty explaining CV projects:
Figure 2 shows that 53.0% of respondents reported difficulty explaining projects included in their CVs. This is a relevant problem for internship and entry-level IT interviews, where candidates may be required to explain their own projects, responsibilities, technical decisions, and contributions.

Need for CV-personalized practice:
Figure 4 shows that 76.7% of respondents rated the necessity of CV-personalized interview practice at level 4 or 5 on the five-point scale. This suggests that respondents consider interview practice based on their own CV, projects, skills, and experience more useful than relying solely on generic interview questions.

Low confidence in speaking:
Figure 2 shows that 55.1% of respondents reported feeling nervous or lacking confidence when speaking. Figure 3 further shows that 51.7% of respondents rarely or never practice answering interview questions aloud. These findings indicate that interview preparation involves not only knowledge acquisition but also spoken communication and performance, supporting the need for a voice-based mock interview environment.

Need for progress tracking:
71.2% of respondents rated the importance of saving interview results for comparison over time at level 4 or 5. This indicates that respondents value measurable progress and want to track their performance across multiple practice sessions rather than relying only on one-time feedback.

Affordable payment willingness:
Figure 5 shows that approximately 69.9% of respondents were willing to pay for an online interview practice system. The most preferred price range was 30,000–50,000 VND per month (38.1%), followed by 50,000–100,000 VND per month (19.9%). These findings suggest that a freemium or low-cost subscription model is more appropriate for the target users.

Figure 2 Percentage of respondents reporting each difficulty during interview preparation.

Figure 3 How often respondents practice answering interview questions aloud

Figure 4 Respondent ratings (1–5) on the necessity of CV-personalized interview practice

Figure 5 Respondent willingness to pay for an online interview practice system

In summary, the survey findings indicate that the lack of a structured, personalized, and feedback-rich practice environment is a significant problem among the surveyed target users. The findings highlight several recurring needs, including reliable feedback after practice, CV-personalized interview questions, opportunities for spoken practice, and the ability to monitor progress over time. The results therefore provide supporting evidence for the need for a structured AI-assisted interview practice system for Vietnamese IT candidates preparing for internships, fresher, and entry-level positions.

1.2.2 HR Stakeholder Interviews

To complement the target-user survey, the project team conducted qualitative interviews with HR and hiring-related stakeholders to understand the employer-side perspective of interview evaluation. One recurring pain point identified from these interviews was the lack of a consistently defined and structured rubric for evaluating interview performance and determining whether a candidate should pass or fail a given interview stage. Evaluation may depend on different criteria such as technical knowledge, problem-solving ability, communication, project understanding, and role requirements, but these criteria are not always translated into a unified scoring and decision framework.

This finding motivates the development of a structured interview evaluation rubric in AI-SPEIS, which defines evaluation criteria, scoring levels, and decision rules to support more consistent AI-assisted assessment.

Figure 6 Representative IT Recruitment and Interview Process Identified from HR Stakeholder Interviews

The HR interviews identified several recurring employer-side pain points. These findings are qualitative and are therefore presented by observed level of occurrence rather than as population-level percentages.

Pain Point | Frequency Level

CV does not match the JD / missing required skills | Very High

CV looks strong, but actual ability does not match | Very High

Weak technical fundamentals | Very High

Weak coding / problem-solving skills | Very High

Unable to explain projects they have worked on | Medium

Weak communication / interview skills | Medium

English proficiency is not sufficient | Medium

These HR interviews indicate that candidate evaluation involves multiple dimensions, including CV–JD fit, technical knowledge, coding and problem-solving ability, project understanding, communication, and English proficiency. However, these dimensions are not always translated into a unified and explicit evaluation framework that clearly defines scoring levels or pass/fail decisions. As a result, the evaluation process may depend on the interviewer’s individual judgment and the specific requirements of each role.

Based on these findings, AI-SPEIS defines a structured interview evaluation rubric that organizes the key evaluation dimensions into explicit criteria, scoring levels, and decision rules. The rubric provides a consistent foundation for evaluating candidate responses and determining interview outcomes, while also serving as controlled knowledge for the AI evaluation component.

The rubric is subsequently used as part of the research baseline to investigate whether a domain-specific fine-tuned model can follow predefined evaluation criteria and decision rules more consistently than a general-purpose AI model.

1.3 Limitations of Existing Solutions

Although respondents already use different methods to prepare for interviews, these approaches do not fully solve the problems identified in the survey. As shown in Figure 7, respondents commonly search for sample interview questions online, watch interview preparation videos, and use ChatGPT or other AI tools.

Figure 7 Percentage of respondents using each preparation method

The main limitations are:

Traditional self-practice is passive:
Google search, blogs, and tutorial videos help respondents collect information, but they do not simulate real interview pressure or provide direct, personalized feedback.

Generic materials lack personalization:
Most sample questions are not based on the candidate’sCV, projects, skills, or target position. Therefore, candidate may still struggle when interviewers ask about their own experience.

General-purpose AI chatbots are not structured interview systems:
Tools such as ChatGPT can generate interview questions, evaluate text, and provide suggestions, but users must manually provide context and manage the interview process themselves. More importantly, general-purpose AI models are designed for broad tasks rather than for a specific interview evaluation policy. They are not inherently constrained by AI-SPEIS's predefined scoring rubrics, interview decision rules, question-bank structure, or expected output format. As a result, similar answers may potentially lead to variations in evaluation, feedback detail, or next-question decisions.

This creates an additional opportunity for AI-SPEIS beyond workflow integration. The project can investigate whether domain-specific fine-tuning helps a language model follow interview-specific evaluation behavior more consistently, while predefined question banks and retrieval mechanisms provide controlled interview content and knowledge.

Existing mock interview platforms are not localized enough:
Platforms such as Pramp, Interviewing.io, and Exponent mainly target international or English-speaking users. They do not fully address Vietnamese-language practice, fresher-level interviews, or the needs of Vietnamese IT candidates preparing for local internship and entry-level recruitment.

Therefore, existing solutions still lack a realistic, personalized, localized, and feedback-driven interview practice environment for Vietnamese IT candidates. This creates an opportunity for AI-SPEIS.

2. Existing Solutions

Students and fresh graduates usually prepare for interviews through two main methods: traditional self-practice and AI-powered mock interview platforms. Traditional methods are easy to access but often passive, generic, and lack feedback. Meanwhile, AI-powered platforms provide more interactive practice, but most of them are designed for international users and do not fully support Vietnamese IT students preparing for internships or fresher positions. Therefore, this section analyzes these existing solutions to identify their strengths, weaknesses, and the gaps that AI-SPEIS can address.

2.1 Traditional Self-Practice and Manual Preparation

Traditional self-practice includes searching interview questions on Google, watching YouTube tutorials, reading sample answers, using ChatGPT, asking friends or seniors, and practicing independently.

Attribute | Description

Solution Type | Manual and self-directed interview preparation

Target Customers | Individual students, fresh graduates, job seekers

Primary Users | Students preparing for internships, fresher jobs, or first full-time positions

Usage Environment | Personal study environment, usually at home, school, dormitory, or library

Common Tools Used | Google Search, YouTube, blogs, interview question lists, ChatGPT, friends, seniors, personal notes

Core Activities | Reading common questions, watching tutorials, preparing sample answers, practicing alone, asking friends for feedback

Table 1 Characteristics of Traditional Self-Practice Methods

Strengths

Traditional self-practice is easy to access, low-cost, and flexible. Students can prepare anytime without depending on a mentor, interviewer, or fixed schedule. It is useful as a starting point because it helps students become familiar with common interview topics such as self-introduction, HR questions, technical questions, behavioral questions, and project explanation.

Weaknesses

However, this method is mostly passive and does not simulate real interview pressure. Students often read or write answers instead of speaking aloud, so they may still struggle when answering in a real interview. It also lacks reliable feedback, CV-based personalization, and progress tracking. As a result, students may not know whether their answers are clear, complete, technically correct, or convincing.

Gap for AI-SPEIS

Traditional self-practice helps students prepare basic content, but it cannot provide a realistic, personalized, feedback-driven, and measurable interview practice experience.

2.2 AI-Powered Mock Interview Platforms

AI-powered mock interview platforms are closer to AI-SPEIS because they provide interview simulation, technical practice, coaching, peer practice, or AI-supported feedback. This section focuses on three relevant systems:

Exponent AI / Exponent

Interviewing.io

Pramp / Exponent Practice

2.2.1 Exponent AI / Exponent

Exponent is a technology interview preparation platform for candidates applying to roles such as software engineering, product management, data science, and system design. It provides courses, mock interviews, coaching, peer practice, resume review, and AI-supported interview preparation.

tryexponent.com

Figure 8 Exponent AI Mock Interview Platform Interface

Attribute | Description

System Type | Technology interview preparation and coaching platform

Target Customers | Individual job seekers, technology candidates, professional candidates

Primary Users | Software engineering candidates, product candidates, data candidates, experienced job seekers

Usage Environment | Web-based preparation environment, usually used individually before real interviews

Core Features | Interview courses, AI interview practice, mock interviews, peer practice, coaching, resume review, behavioral interview preparation

Main Focus | Preparing candidates for technology roles in competitive recruitment markets

Table 2 Overview of Exponent AI Platform

Strengths

Exponent provides a strong preparation ecosystem by combining learning content, mock interviews, coaching, and role-specific preparation. It supports many interview types, including behavioral, technical, product, and system design interviews. Its structured materials also help users learn how to organize answers before practicing.

Weaknesses

Exponent is mainly designed for international and English-speaking candidates. It may be too broad or advanced for Vietnamese IT preparing for internships or fresher jobs. It also does not strongly focus on Vietnamese recruitment contexts, academic projects, or student-level CV explanation. In addition, premium coaching and resources may create a cost barrier for students.

2.2.2 Interviewing.io

Interviewing.io is a technical interview practice platform for software engineering candidates. It focuses on coding interviews, system design interviews, anonymous mock interviews, and technical feedback.

Interviewing.io

Figure 9 Interviewing.io Technical Interview Practice Interface

Attribute | Description

System Type | Technical mock interview practice platform

Target Customers | Software engineering candidates, professional developers, technical job seekers

Primary Users | Candidates preparing for coding interviews, system design interviews, and high-level software engineering roles

Usage Environment | Online technical interview practice environment

Core Features | Anonymous mock interviews, coding interviews, system design interviews, AI interviewer, technical feedback

Main Focus | Realistic software engineering interview practice, especially coding and system design

Table 3 Overview of Interviewing.io Platform

Strengths

Interviewing.io provides a realistic technical interview environment, especially for coding and system design practice. Its anonymous practice format can reduce pressure and help candidates focus on performance. It is useful for candidates targeting competitive software engineering positions and provides feedback after mock interviews.

Weaknesses

The platform may be too advanced for many university students and fresher candidates. It is mainly English-focused and international-market-oriented. It also emphasizes technical problem-solving more than CV-based questions, academic project explanation, behavioral answers, or basic communication improvement, which are important for fresher-level interviews in Vietnam.

2.2.3 Pramp / Exponent Practice

Pramp / Exponent Practice is a peer-to-peer mock interview platform where users are matched with other candidates and take turns as interviewer and interviewee. It focuses on live peer practice, coding interviews, and feedback exchange.

Pramp.com

Figure 10 Pramp Peer-to-Peer Mock Interview Platform

Attribute | Description

System Type | Peer-to-peer mock interview practice platform

Target Customers | Individual candidates and job seekers preparing for interviews

Primary Users | Software engineering candidates, product candidates, data candidates, job seekers

Usage Environment | Online live peer interview environment

Core Features | Peer matching, live mock interviews, role switching, coding practice, peer feedback

Main Focus | Real-time peer-based interview practice and feedback exchange

Table 4 Overview of Pramp / Exponent Practice Platform

Strengths

Pramp / Exponent Practice provides real human interaction, which helps users practice communication under interview-like pressure. The peer learning model is also useful because users can learn by both answering questions and acting as interviewers. This creates a more interactive experience than passive self-practice.

Weaknesses

The quality of feedback depends heavily on the assigned peer. If the peer lacks experience or seriousness, the feedback may be inaccurate or unhelpful. Scheduling and matching can also reduce flexibility. In addition, the platform does not deeply personalize interviews based on the user’s CV, projects, skills, or target position, and it is not localized for Vietnamese IT.

2.2.4 Key Lessons for AI-SPEIS

From these three systems, AI-SPEIS can learn that an effective interview preparation platform should support a complete practice cycle: preparation, interview simulation, feedback, review, and improvement. Exponent shows the value of a structured preparation ecosystem; Interviewing.io shows the importance of realistic technical interview practice; and Pramp / Exponent Practice shows the benefit of peer learning and interaction.

However, AI-SPEIS should adapt these ideas to a more specific target group: Vietnamese IT candidates preparing for internships and fresher-level jobs. Instead of focusing on advanced international recruitment, AI-SPEIS should emphasize CV/project-based personalization, Vietnamese-language support, voice-based practice, rubric-based feedback and progress tracking.

2.3 Improvement Opportunities for AI-SPEIS

Based on the analysis above, AI-SPEIS can improve on existing systems by focusing on a narrower but more suitable target segment: Vietnamese IT candidates preparing for internships and fresher-level positions.

Feature / Capability | Exponent AI / Exponent | Interviewing.io | Pramp / Exponent Practice | AI-SPEIS

Interview practice platform

Vietnamese-language support

CV/JD-based question selection

Adaptive clarification/follow-up selection from controlled Question Bank

Vietnamese Voice-based AI Interaction

Structured AI feedback

Progress tracking

Student-oriented low-cost access

Table 5 Comparison of Existing Interview Preparation Platforms

2.4 Identified Gaps

Based on the analysis of traditional self-practice and AI-powered mock interview platforms, the following gaps are identified. These gap IDs will be used in later sections to map AI-SPEIS features to market limitations.

Gap ID | Gap Description | Explanation

GAP-01 | Lack of realistic interview simulation for early-career IT candidates | Traditional self-practice is mostly passive, while some existing platforms are too advanced or not localized. Students need an accessible mock interview environment that simulates interview pressure, pacing, and question flow.

GAP-02 | Lack of evidence-based clarification and context-aware follow-up questioning | Existing preparation methods often use static question sequences and do not evaluate whether a candidate's answer is ambiguous, partially complete, or sufficiently complete before determining the next interview action. Candidates therefore lack structured clarification and targeted follow-up based on the evidence contained in their previous response.

GAP-03 | Lack of voice-based practice with STT/TTS support | Real interviews require speaking, but many students only read or type answers. AI-SPEIS needs an integrated voice-based flow using Speech-to-text and Text-to-speech.

GAP-04 | Lack of CV/project-based personalization | Generic question banks and many mock interview platforms do not deeply personalize questions based on students’ CVs, projects, skills, and experience.

GAP-05 | Lack of structured feedback and progress tracking | Students need rubric-based scoring, clear suggestions, session history, and progress analytics to know how they improve over time.

GAP-06 | Lack of CV-to-JD matching analysis | Existing platforms evaluate general competency but fail to analyze how well a student's CV matches a specific Job Description (JD). Students need targeted practice based on the exact roles they are applying for.

GAP-07 | Lack of integrated technical coding environments | General AI chatbots cannot host real-time coding interviews. Students need access to integrated IDEs to simulate practical technical screening rounds effectively.

GAP-08 | Lack of behavioral framework (STAR) & delivery analytics | Traditional platforms focus heavily on content but overlook speech delivery. There is a need for behavioral practice guided by the STAR method and speech-delivery analytics, such as filler-word, hesitation, and speech-pacing analysis.

GAP-09 | Lack of operational monitoring and administrative control | AI-powered interview systems consume external AI services and require continuous monitoring of usage, quotas, service errors, and payment activities. Without centralized administrative monitoring, system operators may struggle to control operating costs, identify service failures, and manage abnormal payment or quota activities.

GAP-10 | Lack of affordable and sustainable access for Vietnamese IT candidates | Many existing interview preparation platforms may be costly for Vietnamese students, while AI-powered practice consumes paid external services. Students need an affordable access model, and the system needs mechanisms to balance user affordability with operating costs.

GAP-11 | Lack of domain-Specific AI Evaluation | General-purpose AI models are not specifically optimized for predefined interview evaluation criteria and decision rules. AI-SPEIS investigates whether domain-specific fine-tuning can improve the consistency, rule adherence, and reliability of structured outputs.

Table 6 Identified Gaps in Existing Interview Preparation Solutions

3. Proposed Solution

AI-SPEIS is an AI-integrated interview practice and evaluation platform that helps IT candidates prepare in a structured, realistic, and personalized way. Unlike existing solutions that lack personalized interview practice, detailed post-interview feedback, and progress tracking, AI-SPEIS supports students throughout the interview preparation process, from CV analysis and personalized question selection to mock interview practice and performance evaluation.

The main beneficiaries of this project are students and people who are preparing for internships, fresher positions, or their first full-time jobs. They will be helped by having a professional environment to practice interviews repeatedly, understand their weaknesses, improve their communication and technical explanation skills, and monitor their progress over time. In addition, educational institutions also benefit from the project by having a practical tool to support students in career preparation before internships or job applications, which will improve the quality of their students.

This is the right approach because interview preparation is increasingly important for students, while access to real interview practice or professional coaching is often limited. A system that combines mock interview practice, personalized evaluation, progress tracking, and controlled access through service packages creates a more scalable and sustainable solution than traditional manual practice. It allows students to practice more frequently and receive consistent feedback without depending entirely on human reviewers. In addition, students are becoming more familiar with digital learning platforms and AI-assisted tools. Moreover, employers expect candidates to demonstrate not only knowledge but also clear communication, confidence, and the ability to explain their experience effectively. AI-SPEIS fits this need by turning interview preparation into a measurable, repeatable, and accessible learning process.

In parallel with the development of the functional interview platform, AI-SPEIS also includes an applied AI research track. The product track uses a general-purpose external AI model as a practical baseline for the interview workflow, while the research track explores domain-specific fine-tuning of a pretrained language model. These two approaches are developed and evaluated in parallel to investigate whether model adaptation can provide measurable benefits for interview-specific tasks while also considering implementation complexity, computational requirements, and other practical trade-offs.

3.1 Research Objective

In addition to developing a practical AI-assisted interview preparation platform, AI-SPEIS includes an applied AI research component that investigates domain-specific language-model fine-tuning for interview evaluation and decision-making tasks. The research has two complementary purposes: to gain practical experience in preparing interview-specific datasets, adapting a pretrained language model, and evaluating model behavior, and to empirically compare the fine-tuned model with a general-purpose external AI model under controlled interview scenarios.

The research aims to determine whether a fine-tuned model can provide more consistent, rule-aligned, and structured interview reasoning than a general-purpose external AI model when both approaches are evaluated under the same controlled interview scenarios.

Specifically, the research focuses on the following objectives:

Evaluate the consistency of AI-based answer evaluation across different interview responses.

Evaluate adherence to predefined scoring rubrics and interview decision rules.

Evaluate the reliability of structured AI outputs required by the system.

Evaluate model behavior when handling incomplete, partially correct, incorrect, off-topic, or abnormal interview responses.

Compare the interview-domain alignment of the fine-tuned model with the general-purpose external AI baseline.

Identify the practical advantages, limitations, and trade-offs of applying fine-tuning within an AI-assisted interview system.

The objective is not to assume that fine-tuning will necessarily outperform a general-purpose model. Instead, the project seeks to provide empirical evidence regarding when domain-specific model adaptation is beneficial for AI-assisted interview evaluation.

3.2 AI Approach and Research Direction

AI-SPEIS separates domain knowledge from model behavior to ensure controllable and consistent interview evaluation. Interview questions, expected answers, rubrics, and related context are stored in structured data sources and accessed through retrieval mechanisms. The AI model then reasons over this context to perform tasks such as answer evaluation, interview decision making, question selection, feedback generation, and handling abnormal responses.

During development, a general-purpose external AI model is used as the baseline. In parallel, a domain-specific fine-tuned model is trained on structured AI-SPEIS interview datasets. Both models are evaluated under the same interview scenarios and criteria.

The goal is not to assume fine-tuning is superior, but to empirically assess whether it improves evaluation consistency, rule adherence, structured output reliability, and domain alignment, while also identifying its limitations and trade-offs.

The system architecture consists of three components:

Controlled interview knowledge: question banks, rubrics, expected answers, and candidate context

Retrieval mechanisms: provide relevant interview information to the model

AI reasoning model: either a general-purpose baseline or a fine-tuned model for comparison

This design enables controlled interview content while evaluating whether model adaptation improves the reliability of AI-driven interview behavior.

4. Project Scope & Limitations

4.1 Major Features

ID | Feature Name | Description | Addresses Gap

FE-01 | Structured Multi-Round AI Interview Engine with Evidence-Based Follow-up Logic | The system conducts structured AI-driven interview sessions using confirmed CV and analyzed JD context. For eligible spoken-answer questions, the system evaluates the candidate's response against predefined expected evidence and rubric criteria and selects one bounded next action: ask a clarification question, ask a relevant follow-up question, or proceed to the next question. Open-ended adaptive interviewing is excluded from the MVP. | GAP-01, GAP-02, GAP-08

FE-02 | Automated Audio Processing Subsystem | Integrates STT/TTS for vocal interaction and actively analyzes spoken response delivery, including the detection of filler words and speech pacing, to provide communication coaching. | GAP-01, GAP-03,

GAP-08

FE-03 | Smart CV/JD Parsing & Matching Analytics | Extracts data from uploaded CVs and Job Descriptions (JDs). Performs a CV-to-JD Fast Check & Matching Analysis to dynamically personalize the interview based on the specific job requirements. | GAP-04, GAP-06

FE-04 | Comprehensive Evaluation & Skill Dashboard | Provides diagnostic reports with rubric-based scoring, strength/weakness breakdowns, alternative sample answers, session history, and visualized skill progress over time. | GAP-05

FE-05 | Centralized Question Bank & Selection | Hosts a repository of categorized interview questions and utilizes LLM support to select domain-specific questions from question bank, moving beyond static and theoretical self-study lists. User can select active saved question to start Single Question Mode | GAP-01, GAP-02

FE-06 | Subscription, Payment, and Quota Management | Provides a freemium/pro subscription model with interview quotas. Users can upgrade their accounts through the MoMo Developer Sandbox payment gateway. After a payment is successfully verified in the sandbox environment, the system updates the user’s subscription status and available interview quota. The system also tracks quota consumption to control AI service usage and operating costs. | GAP-09,

GAP-10

FE-07 | Account, Role, and Profile Management | Provides account registration, login, authentication, role-based access control, user profile management, and basic security settings. This feature ensures that students and admins can access the correct functions and that profile information can be used to support personalized interview practice. | GAP-04, GAP-05

FE-08 | Reward Points & Premium Discount System | Provides reward points earned strictly through the completion of AI interview sessions. Accumulated points can be directly applied as a billing discount to reduce the payment amount when upgrading to a Pro/Premium subscription. The system applies anti-abuse rules to prevent point exploitation. | GAP-10

FE-09 | Notification and Transactional Email | Provides in-system notifications and important transactional emails, such as premium registration confirmation, payment-related messages, and system notifications. This feature helps users stay informed about interview results, subscription changes, quota status, and important account activities. | GAP-05

FE-10 | Admin Operations | Allows administrators to monitor AI service usage, track quota consumption, review recorded service errors, and monitor payment activities. | GAP-09

FE-11 | Integrated Coding Interview via External IDE | Facilitates real-time coding interviews by integrating an external IDE, allowing candidates to write, execute, and explain code under interview conditions. | GAP-07

FE-12 | Pre-Interview Device Readiness Check | Ensures system stability by requiring users to complete a microphone, audio, and device readiness check before initiating an AI interview session. | GAP-01

FE-13 | AI Evaluation Feedback System | Allows users to flag inaccurate AI gradings and submit feedback on the AI evaluation, providing a mechanism to continuously improve the system's assessment accuracy. | GAP-05

Table 7 Major Features of AI-SPEIS

Research and AI Evaluation Scope

In addition to the functional product scope, AI-SPEIS includes an applied AI research scope focused on domain-specific language-model adaptation. This research scope covers the preparation of structured interview datasets, fine-tuning of a selected pretrained language model, development of controlled evaluation data, and comparative evaluation between the fine-tuned model and a general-purpose external AI baseline.

The comparison focuses on interview-specific tasks such as answer evaluation, interview decision making, question selection, feedback generation, and edge-case handling. The research is intended to evaluate the effectiveness of fine-tuning within the defined AI-SPEIS interview domain rather than to develop or train a foundation language model from scratch.

4.2 Limitations & Exclusions

ID | Excluded Item | Reason

LI-01 | Real-Time Video/ Image Processing | Video-based interview analysis, including facial expression tracking, eye-contact detection, and body language analysis, is excluded from the MVP to reduce project complexity.

LI-02 | Native iOS/Android Mobile Applications | The system will be built entirely as a Responsive Web Application using ReactJS. Developing native apps requires independent mobile codebases, which exceeds the scope and resource allocation of the development cohort.

LI-03 | Live Peer-to-Peer Interview Streaming | Live video/audio streaming between peers or real-time mentor-student calls is excluded due to high WebRTC server infrastructure costs.

LI-04 | Direct Banking Gateway & Refund Automation | The MVP integrates with MoMo Developer Sandbox to simulate and verify the payment workflow. Real-money transactions, production payment processing, and automated refunds are excluded from the MVP because they require production merchant approval, legal compliance, and financial risk management.

LI-05 | Offline AI Model Execution | All heavy processing, including layout extraction, transcription (Google Cloud Speech-to-Text), and response assessment, relies entirely on cloud-based LLM endpoints. The platform will not support local or offline processing due to client-side hardware constraints.

LI-06 | Proprietary Code Compiler & Execution Environment | While coding interviews are supported, the system will integrate an External IDE rather than building a custom code compiler/execution sandbox from scratch, in order to maintain MVP feasibility and security.

LI-07 | Flashcard Practice Module | Originally considered for quick theoretical preparation, the flashcard module has been explicitly excluded from the MVP scope. The development resources are strictly reallocated toward high-value, realistic simulation features (such as Multi-Round interviews, Coding IDE integration, and Audio Analytics).

LI-08 | Community Features and Public Content Sharing | Community features, including public posts, comments, reactions, discussion threads, and public sharing of interview scores or achievements, are excluded from the MVP. This decision keeps the project focused on the core AI interview practice and evaluation workflow, reduces moderation and privacy risks, and ensures that development resources are allocated to higher-priority interview features.

LI-09 | Fine-Tuned Model Scope and Generalization | The fine-tuned model is optimized for the interview tasks, datasets, rubrics, and decision rules defined within AI-SPEIS. Performance outside the supported interview domain is not a primary objective of the project. Due to limitations in available training data and computing resources, the research focuses on adapting an existing pretrained language model rather than training a foundation model from scratch.

Table 8 Project Limitations and Exclusions

Canonical Full Interview Lifecycle

Stage | Purpose | Main input | Main output

CV/JD Screening | Determine relevance and context. | CV + JD | Match evidence, gaps, context

Behavioral | STAR rating, ownership, reflection | Voice/text answer | Behavioral evaluation

Technical | Assessing technical correctness and reasoning | CV, JD, question, answer | Technical evaluation

Coding | Evaluate the ability to solve the code problem. | Code submission | Judge result

Final Assessment | Summary of the entire session | Round results | Overall score, strengths, gaps, recommendations

5. Expected Contributions & Next Steps

Based on the survey findings, analysis of existing solutions, and the identified AI evaluation challenges, AI-SPEIS is expected to contribute in two complementary dimensions: a practical interview preparation platform and an applied AI research study. From the product perspective, the system provides a localized, personalized, and feedback-driven interview preparation environment for Vietnamese IT candidates. It helps students practice interviews more realistically, receive structured feedback, and track their improvement before applying for internships or fresher positions. From the research perspective, AI-SPEIS investigates whether domain-specific language-model fine-tuning can improve the consistency, rule adherence, structured-output reliability, and interview-domain alignment of AI-assisted interview evaluation compared with a general-purpose AI baseline.

5.1 Business & Operational Impact

AI-SPEIS is expected to create business and operational value by centralizing the interview preparation process into one integrated platform. Currently, respondents prepare through fragmented methods such as searching online, watching tutorial videos, asking friends, or using general-purpose AI tools. According to the survey, 64.0% of respondents search for sample interview questions online, 44.9% watch interview preparation videos, and 45.8% use ChatGPT or other AI tools. However, these methods are mostly passive and do not provide a complete interview simulation and evaluation workflow.

By combining CV analysis, personalized question selection, AI interview simulation, answer evaluation, feedback generation, and progress tracking, AI-SPEIS can reduce the need for students to use multiple separate tools. Instead of using one platform for sample questions, another platform for AI chat, and another person for feedback, students can complete the main preparation workflow inside one system.

From an operational perspective, AI-SPEIS can also reduce the dependency on manual feedback from mentors, peers, or teachers. The survey shows that 62.7% of respondents reported lacking someone to provide feedback after answering interview questions, while 58.9% reported difficulty determining whether their answers were appropriate. With AI-based answer evaluation, the system can provide immediate initial feedback on technical correctness, clarity, structure, completeness, and relevance to the student’s CV. This allows students to practice more frequently without always waiting for human reviewers.

Compared with existing mock interview platforms such as Pramp / Exponent Practice, Interviewing.io, and Exponent AI, AI-SPEIS is more suitable for the Vietnamese IT market. These international platforms are strong in technical mock interviews, peer practice, coding interviews, and preparation for global software engineering roles. However, their main limitations are the use of English as the dominant language, higher difficulty level, possible cost barriers, and limited alignment with local internship or fresher recruitment in Vietnam. AI-SPEIS can address this gap by supporting Vietnamese IT, focusing on CV/project-based questions, and designing the interview flow around entry-level IT recruitment needs.

In future versions, AI-SPEIS could be extended to support universities, career centers, and IT training programs in organizing interview preparation activities and monitoring student readiness with appropriate user consent. In the long term, AI-SPEIS can support a scalable preparation model where AI handles the basic practice and feedback process, while mentors focus on deeper guidance and final evaluation.

Figure 11 AI-SPEIS Interview Practice and Evaluation Workflow

5.2 User Experience Impact

AI-SPEIS is expected to significantly improve the user experience of interview preparation by making it more personalized, interactive, and measurable.

First, students can receive interview questions based not only on their own CV but also on a specific Job Description (JD). Through CV-to-JD matching analysis, AI-SPEIS identifies skill gaps and selects highly relevant questions. This allows students to practice Multi-Round formats—ranging from Technical Deep-Dives and External IDE Coding challenges to Behavioral rounds guided by the STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) framework. This holistic approach directly mirrors enterprise screening processes.

Second, AI-SPEIS pushes beyond just recognizing text. The integration of Speech-to-Text now includes spoken response delivery analysis, identifying filler words and hesitations. This ensures students improve both what they say and how they deliver it, directly boosting their confidence (addressing the 55.1% who feel nervous).

Third, the integration of Speech-to-Text and Text-to-Speech can help students practice speaking more naturally. This directly addresses the issue that 55.1% of students experience nervousness or lack of confidence when speaking, and 51.7% rarely or never practice answering questions aloud. Voice-based practice helps students improve fluency, confidence, response speed, and the ability to organize ideas under time pressure.

Fourth, AI-SPEIS provides immediate and actionable feedback after each answer. The feedback may include strengths, weaknesses, missing points, unclear explanations, technical inaccuracies, and suggestions for improvement. This helps students understand not only whether their answer is good or bad, but also how to improve it. For example, the system can point out that an answer lacks a concrete example, does not explain personal contribution clearly, or does not connect well with the student’s CV.

Fifth, the system improves the long-term learning experience through practice history and progress analytics. Since 71.2% of respondents wanted the system to save session results for comparison over time, AI-SPEIS can help students track their improvement across multiple sessions. Students can review previous answers, compare scores, identify repeated weaknesses, and focus on specific areas such as project explanation, behavioral questions, technical knowledge, or communication clarity.

In terms of language and accessibility, AI-SPEIS is expected to be more user-friendly for Vietnamese IT candidates than many international mock interview platforms. Existing platforms such as Pramp, Interviewing.io, and Exponent are useful for students with strong English skills and global job targets, but they may be difficult for students who are still preparing for local internships or fresher roles. By supporting Vietnamese language interaction and focusing on student-level interview scenarios, AI-SPEIS can reduce the barrier to entry and make interview practice more accessible to a wider group of users in Vietnam.

Overall, AI-SPEIS is expected to replace isolated and passive interview preparation with a personalized, interactive, voice-based, and feedback-driven practice experience.

Figure 12 Respondent Demand for AI-SPEIS Core Features

The survey also examined respondents' willingness to pay for an online interview practice platform. Among the 236 respondents, approximately 69.9% indicated willingness to pay. The most preferred price range was 30,000–50,000 VND/month (38.1%), followed by 50,000–100,000 VND/month (19.9%). These findings provide initial support for a freemium or low-cost subscription model, with the paid tier positioned within an affordable range for the target users. .

5.3 Research & Technical Contribution

In addition to its practical contribution as an interview preparation platform, AI-SPEIS provides an applied research contribution in the use of domain-specific language-model adaptation for interview evaluation.

First, the project develops structured datasets representing key AI-assisted interview tasks, including answer evaluation, interview decision making, question selection and planning, final interview feedback, and edge-case handling. These datasets translate the expected interview behavior, evaluation rules, and decision logic of AI-SPEIS into structured examples that can support model adaptation and controlled evaluation.

Second, the project investigates an AI architecture in which controlled interview knowledge is separated from learned model behavior. Question banks, expected-answer information, evaluation rubrics, and relevant candidate context remain controlled sources of information, while the language model performs reasoning and produces structured interview decisions. This approach allows fine-tuning to focus on adapting model behavior without requiring the model to memorize the complete interview knowledge base.

Third, AI-SPEIS conducts a comparative evaluation between a domain-specific fine-tuned model and a general-purpose external AI baseline. Both approaches are evaluated using comparable test scenarios and common evaluation criteria. The comparison focuses on answer-evaluation quality, decision consistency, rule adherence, structured-output reliability, domain alignment, and robustness when handling abnormal or incomplete interview inputs.

Finally, the research aims to identify not only the potential benefits of fine-tuning but also its limitations and trade-offs, including dependency on dataset quality, computing requirements, domain generalization, and model maintenance. The resulting findings can provide practical evidence for determining when domain-specific fine-tuning is appropriate for AI-assisted interview systems and when a general-purpose model combined with controlled context and retrieval mechanisms may be sufficient.

5.4 Planned Next Steps After Project Completion

After the first version of AI-SPEIS is completed, the system should be validated through a simulated interview preparation process with university students, especially IT students who are preparing for internships or entry-level jobs. The validation should cover the complete user flow, including CV upload, CV parsing, personalized question selection from the controlled Question Bank, AI interview simulation, voice-based answering, answer evaluation, feedback display, practice history tracking, and progress analytics.

The first next step is to conduct user testing with students from the target group. Since the original survey already shows strong demand for personalized and feedback-based interview practice, the next validation should focus on whether students find the system useful, understandable, realistic, and easy to use. Important evaluation criteria may include question relevance, feedback usefulness, speech interaction quality, user confidence after practice, and willingness to reuse the system.

The second next step is to improve the AI-assisted question selection and planning logic. The current version selects interview questions from the controlled Question Bank using candidate context, question metadata, and interview configuration. Future research may investigate controlled question generation, but such generated content is outside the current MVP question-source rule.

The third next step is to enhance the answer evaluation module. Future versions can use more advanced scoring criteria, including technical accuracy, answer completeness, logical structure, communication clarity, confidence, keyword coverage, relevance to the CV, and suitability for the target position. This will help the system provide more reliable and detailed feedback.

The fourth next step is to expand peer and mentor review features. Although AI feedback can provide immediate support, human review is still valuable for deeper evaluation. The system can allow students to share interview sessions with peers, mentors, or lecturers. Reviewers can add comments, give ratings, and compare their feedback with the AI evaluation. This can create a more complete learning ecosystem.

The fifth next step is to improve progress analytics. After more practice data is collected, AI-SPEIS can provide deeper insights such as frequently missed question types, repeated communication weaknesses, technical knowledge gaps, progress trends, and readiness scores for specific job positions. These analytics can help both students and mentors understand the student’s development over time.

The final next step is to evaluate the feasibility of scaling AI-SPEIS in the Vietnamese education and training market. The platform can be extended for use by universities, career centers, IT training programs, and student communities. In the long term, AI-SPEIS can become not only an interview practice tool, but also a broader employability support platform that helps students improve communication, self-presentation, and career readiness.
